analysis.one_liner: Banned tobacco advertising and promotion children could see or hear, and cigarette vending machines where minors go.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 18 cosponsors and one subcommittee hearing, the bill never came to a vote and died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned tobacco companies from running sales promotions — TV and radio spots, billboards, event sponsorships, brand merchandise, movie placements, and samples — anywhere a person under 18 could see or hear them. Print ads would have survived only in stripped-down, text-only form, and billboards would have been phased out by the end of 1991. It also would have banned cigarette vending machines in any place minors can lawfully enter, let anyone sue violators for damages with attorney's fees paid, and required an ongoing independent federal study of what is actually in cigarette smoke.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers, who would have grown up seeing far less tobacco marketing — a population in which, per the bill's findings, more than half of smokers born since 1950 started before 18. Families and consumers would also benefit from fewer tobacco ads at sports venues and stores, and from annual public reporting on tar, nicotine, carbon monoxide, and other smoke constituents. Smokers trying to quit would get more accurate product information, since remaining ads could only state tar, nicotine, and carbon monoxide levels.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children and teens targeted by tobacco marketing

how_it_helps.text: Bans all tobacco sales promotion — commercials, billboards, posters, samples, event sponsorships, brand-name merchandise, and paid movie placements — wherever anyone under 18 could see or hear it, with an exception only for plain, text-only print and billboard ads limited to the package image and tar, nicotine, and carbon monoxide levels.

Outlaws cigarette vending machines in any place a person under 18 may lawfully enter, and requires stores to post a conspicuous sign that selling cigarettes to minors is strictly prohibited — closing a channel children could buy from with no clerk checking age.

Lets any person sue violators in state or federal court for damages and other relief, treats violations as Federal Trade Commission Act violations, and awards attorney's fees to winning plaintiffs — so enforcement would not depend on federal regulators acting first.

Requires the FTC to arrange a continuing, independent study — by a government or nonprofit lab with no tobacco-company ties — of tar, nicotine, carbon monoxide, ammonia, cyanide, formaldehyde, and radioactive compounds in cigarette smoke, with annual reports to Congress, ending industry control over the data used for 'light' and 'low-tar' claims.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, which the bill's findings said spent over $2 billion on advertising and promotion in 1986, would have lost most of the channels they used to recruit new customers. Outdoor advertising companies would have lost tobacco billboard revenue by the end of 1991, sports and event sponsors would have lost brand-name tobacco sponsorship money, and retailers who sold cigarettes from vending machines would have had to switch to over-the-counter sales with a posted warning sign.

drawbacks.text: The restrictions were sweeping for a lawful adult product: even surviving print ads had to be black text on white with a plain package image, and all tobacco billboards were slated to end by December 31, 1991 — close to a total ban on visible tobacco advertising, which raises commercial free-speech objections courts have recognized for regulated advertising.

The bill preempts state and local governments from requiring any tobacco warning that differs from the federal one, so a state wanting stronger or different warning language could not adopt it — a ceiling on state action that public-health officials in tobacco-control states might have opposed.

Retailers would have borne compliance costs: removing vending machines from premises minors can enter, posting required signs, and facing private lawsuits with fee-shifting that create litigation exposure for ordinary store owners as well as manufacturers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case was strong on the bill's own findings: tobacco was described as the largest preventable cause of death, killing over 390,000 Americans a year, costing an estimated $22 billion in 1985 health spending, and reaching children through ads and unattended vending machines. The main costs — lost promotional revenue for tobacco companies, billboard firms, and event sponsors — fall on businesses whose product drives that toll, though honest supporters would concede the near-total ad ban swept beyond clearly child-directed marketing, and the preemption clause would have blocked states from setting stronger warning rules.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee, got a single subcommittee hearing, was never brought to a markup or floor vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Luken introduced the bill on March 2, 1989, joined by Reps. Whittaker and Bates, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
Eleven days later it was split between two subcommittees — Health and the Environment, and Transportation and Hazardous Materials — the only action taken besides one hearing.
A subcommittee hearing was held on July 25, 1989; no markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed.
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 with the bill still in committee, so it never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers kept every promotional channel the bill would have closed — billboards, sponsorships, brand merchandise, and vending machines in places minors enter — and billboard and event-marketing businesses kept the tobacco revenue. Children and teens got none of the protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco companies kept unrestricted marketing channels

for.name: Rep. Thomas A. Luken
for.role: U.S. Representative, Ohio's 2nd district; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through referral and a single subcommittee hearing.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee markup or the House floor; after one subcommittee hearing on July 25, 1989, the bill took no further action.

against.name: Tobacco manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on tobacco advertising, promotion, and vending-machine sales during the late-1980s congressional tobacco-control debates.

against.name: Outdoor advertising industry
against.role: Billboard companies and their trade association
against.what_they_did: Opposed bans and phase-outs of tobacco billboards, which were a major revenue source.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship crossed party lines — 14 Democrats and 4 of the chamber's 175 Republicans signed on — but no vote was ever taken, so the chamber's actual split on the bill is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would have eliminated most of the industry's promotional channels — image ads, billboards, sponsorships, brand merchandise, and samples — wherever minors could see them, and its findings blamed industry promotion for recruiting the majority of smokers who start before 18. What the industry loses, children would have gained.

All tobacco billboards not reduced to plain text were to be banned after December 31, 1991, cutting a revenue stream billboard companies had long defended. Their income depended on promoting a product the bill's findings called the leading preventable cause of death.

Vending machine tobacco sales would have been banned anywhere minors may lawfully enter, forcing a switch to over-the-counter sales with posted warnings and opening owners to private lawsuits for violations.

The bill would have barred tobacco-brand sponsorship of athletic and artistic events (grandfathering certain pre-1988 corporate names), ending a funding stream for events while removing tobacco branding from venues children attend.
